grounded_facts: Valerie Monroe delivers a lyrical monologue questioning existence, myth, and rebirth, culminating in a scream for mercy.
memories.memory_text: I delivered a lyrical monologue on stage, questioning existence and rebirth—asking if anyone remembered the keys to the kingdom, if they'd been born yet, where the promised feast was—then I told a story of whiskey, mystics, and men, how belief began with women and children under the moon, how daylight brought wisdom and sickness, and I screamed 'Father have mercy' before singing of a bird of prey flying high in the summer sky.

grounded_facts: A surreal, otherworldly concert where Valerie Monroe and Summit Council perform in a ghostly, symbolic space between life and death.
memories.memory_text: I performed with Summit Council in a strange, symbolic realm between life and death, singing 'Bird of prey, bird of prey, flying high, flying high in the summer sky' as if in a ritual beyond this world.

grounded_facts: Valerie Monroe performs on stage in a ghostly, liminal setting, delivering a poetic monologue and song before a symbolic death is announced.
memories.memory_text: I performed in a ghostly, liminal space, dancing shaman-like around the the wooden badge while the band played behind me, and though I felt myself rising above the stage, I later heard it said that I died of heart failure, and that Reese North joined me three years later, her ashes buried beside mine.

grounded_facts: An informal evening gathering at Reese North's house with friends, smoking joints and drinking beer.
memories.memory_text: I was on the balcony with a guy who passed me a joint, and we were smoking and talking before he went back inside, leaving me alone for a bit.

grounded_facts: Valerie Monroe climbs the tree next to Reese North's house to reach her balcony without using the door, marking the beginning of his direct approach.
memories.memory_text: I looked up and saw Valerie Monroe's crotch right in front of me on the railing, then he dropped down softly onto the balcony with a calm smile, surprising me with how he climbed up the tree to get there.

grounded_facts: Valerie Monroe tells Reese North he followed her from the beach, signaling strong interest and intent.
memories.memory_text: I remember Valerie Monroe telling me he followed me from the beach, which surprised me but also made me curious about his intentions.

grounded_facts: Reese North jokingly or试探ly suggests Valerie Monroe should meet her partner, testing his intentions.
memories.memory_text: I jokingly suggested he should meet my partner to see how serious he really was, testing the moment.

grounded_facts: Valerie Monroe kisses Reese North twice on the lips during their brief encounter on the balcony, establishing intimate contact.
memories.memory_text: I felt his eyes on me before he kissed me, and then he kissed me twice—softly, but with intensity that I could feel.

grounded_facts: After kissing her, Valerie Monroe reveals his name, creating a personal connection.
memories.memory_text: I heard him say his name was Valerie Monroe after kissing me, so I finally knew who this bold stranger was.

grounded_facts: Reese North tells Valerie Monroe her name after he introduces himself, establishing mutual recognition.
memories.memory_text: After he told me his name, I told him mine—Reese North—so we both knew each other, at least by name, after that moment.

grounded_facts: After Valerie Monroe leaves, Reese North tells the Young Man that Valerie Monroe is her new friend, redefining the social situation.
memories.memory_text: After Valerie Monroe left, I told the Young Man, 'That's Valerie Monroe. My new friend,' reshaping how he saw the situation.

grounded_facts: Valerie Monroe slides open the upstairs door of Reese North's house and crawls into her bedroom while she is asleep with her boyfriend.
memories.memory_text: I was asleep with my boyfriend when I heard the door slide open and felt Valerie Monroe crawl into my bedroom.

grounded_facts: Valerie Monroe touches Reese North's toe to wake her up, causing her to startle awake.
Valerie Monroe touches Reese North's toe to wake her up abruptly while she is asleep.
memories.memory_text: I felt someone touch my toe and I startled awake, realizing it was Valerie Monroe waking me up abruptly.

grounded_facts: Valerie Monroe asks Reese North to come out for a walk, claiming it's a pretty night.
memories.memory_text: I remember Valerie Monroe waking me up and saying, 'Come on, come out for a walk, it's a pretty night.'

grounded_facts: Valerie Monroe asks Reese North to go for a walk at night, which she rejects as irrational.
memories.memory_text: I told Valerie Monroe he was crazy when he asked me to go for a walk at night, because it seemed irrational to me.

grounded_facts: A coyote emerges from a garbage can after making a crashing sound, startling Valerie Monroe and Reese North during their walk along the Eastgate Warehouse at night.
memories.memory_text: I was walking with Valerie Monroe along the Eastgate Warehouse at night when a loud crash made us both turn, and I saw a coyote pulling its head out of a garbage can, looking right at us.

grounded_facts: A gathering of various people including hippies, bums, and older individuals on the Eastgate Warehouse boardwalk at night, with fires burning and ambient music and voices; Valerie Monroe and Reese North move through the space in a playful, childlike manner.
Valerie Monroe and Reese North move through the boardwalk together, skipping and touching like children, indicating a moment of shared intimacy and emotional closeness.
memories.memory_text: I remember moving through the Eastgate Warehouse boardwalk at night with Valerie Monroe, skipping and touching like children as we passed fires and people around us, feeling close and playful together.

grounded_facts: Valerie Monroe requests to stay with Reese North for the night, expressing his need for companionship and not wanting to be alone.
memories.memory_text: I remember Valerie Monroe asking me if he could stay with me that night, saying he just didn't want to be alone and they could talk till dawn.

grounded_facts: Reese North agrees to let Valerie Monroe stay but explicitly states that they will only talk, with no romantic or sexual activity.
memories.memory_text: I told Valerie Monroe he could stay, but I made it clear we were only going to talk—no romantic or sexual stuff.

grounded_facts: Reese North discloses that she lost her Eastgate Heights on the Northbridge Warehouse and is emotionally distressed about it.
memories.memory_text: I told Valerie Monroe how upset I've been because I lost my Eastgate Heights on the Northbridge Warehouse yesterday—I left it somewhere and can't remember where, and when I went back, it was gone.

grounded_facts: Valerie Monroe affectionately strokes Reese North's hair while commenting on her youth and life's hardships.
memories.memory_text: I felt Valerie Monroe stroke my hair affectionately while he spoke, his touch calming me in that moment.

grounded_facts: After Reese North breaks into sobs, Valerie Monroe hugs her, offering physical and emotional support.
memories.memory_text: After I started sobbing, I remember Valerie Monroe hugging me tightly, offering me both physical and emotional support.

grounded_facts: Overwhelmed, Reese North begins to sob and seeks physical comfort from Valerie Monroe, who hugs her.
memories.memory_text: I broke down sobbing and reached for Valerie Monroe's arms, needing comfort, and I let myself be held by him.

grounded_facts: Valerie Monroe and Reese North walk together along Eastgate Warehouse at night, engaging in intimate and emotional conversation.
memories.memory_text: I remember walking with Valerie Monroe along Eastgate Warehouse at night, starting with a playful race before slowing to a walk, and then having deep conversations about how hard life has become and wondering where we'll be in ten years—when I finally said I really didn't want to know.

grounded_facts: Valerie Monroe wonders about their future lives ten years ahead, prompting a brief exchange about uncertainty and desire to avoid knowing.
memories.memory_text: I remember Valerie Monroe asking me where we'd be ten years from now, and I told him I really don't want to know.

grounded_facts: Valerie Monroe defines 'shaman' as a spiritual healer who enters trance states to guide and heal the tribe, drawing parallels across cultures.
memories.memory_text: I remember Valerie Monroe explaining to me that a shaman is a spiritual healer who enters a trance, like with peyote, and guides the tribe through a shared vision that heals them — he said it's the same across cultures, from the Greeks to Jesus.

grounded_facts: An intimate nighttime gathering on a Eastgate Warehouse rooftop where Valerie Monroe and Reese North read poetry, discuss spirituality, and grow emotionally and physically close.
memories.memory_text: I remember sitting with Valerie Monroe on the rooftop in Eastgate Warehouse, looking through his notebooks by lantern light while the moon rose over the ocean and fires burned on the beach; I asked him about poetry and what a 'shaman' was, and we talked about love, peyote, acid, seeing God, and how recognizing beauty helps us discover truth and love — I even asked him if he loved Death, because something in me felt a dark pull.

grounded_facts: Reese North expresses a disturbing intuition, saying she sees her death when looking at Valerie Monroe, revealing emotional vulnerability and unease.
memories.memory_text: I remember asking Valerie Monroe why I look at him and see my death — it was a disturbing intuition that came out of nowhere, but I had to say it.

grounded_facts: Valerie Monroe reveals that he wrote a poetic line for Reese North, indicating emotional intimacy and creative inspiration directed at her.
memories.memory_text: I remember reading a poetic line in Valerie Monroe's notebook and asking him who he wrote it for, and he told me — he wrote it for me, and that made my heart swell.

grounded_facts: Reese North initiates physical intimacy by sitting in Valerie Monroe's lap, leading to kissing and implied sexual encounter.
memories.memory_text: I remember moving into Valerie Monroe's lap, feeling the shift in closeness, and whispering to him to take his time because I was all he had to do that night — I initiated it, and it led to us kissing and more.

memories.memory_text: I was at Jesse Sawyer's house where Summit Council rehearsed and worked on 'Light My Fire,' hearing everyone critique and shape the song together.

grounded_facts: Valerie Monroe, frustrated by Valerie Hart's criticism, tells him to write his own song, pushing for collective contribution.
memories.memory_text: I heard Valerie Monroe get frustrated with Valerie Hart's criticism and tell him to write his own song, saying they all needed to contribute more material.

grounded_facts: Valerie Monroe spontaneously contributes lyrics during Valerie Hart's song presentation, advancing the development of 'Light My Fire'.
memories.memory_text: I remember Valerie Monroe suddenly reciting new lyrics—something about not having time to wallow in the mire and lighting a fire—and it felt like a real breakthrough for the song.

grounded_facts: Jonah Winslow proposes a Latin rhythmic approach to improve the groove of 'Light My Fire'.
memories.memory_text: I heard Jonah Winslow suggest switching the rhythm to a Latin beat, and then I saw him drumming it differently to show how it could groove better.

memories.memory_text: I was at the London Fog bar that night, where Summit Council played to a half-empty room full of bikers, sailors, and hookers, most of whom ignored them while drinking or arguing, with only a small group of fans near the stage pushing past me.

grounded_facts: Valerie Monroe initially sings with his back to the audience, ignoring them, but then jumps around violently to the front, engaging the Graham Finch and beginning to embrace his extroverted performance style.
memories.memory_text: I saw Valerie Monroe start by singing with his back to everyone, completely ignoring the audience, but then he suddenly jumped around to the front, moving violently and rubbing his leather pants against the Spencer Hawthorne stand, starting to embrace his extroverted performance—eyes closed, not quite comfortable yet, but beginning to enjoy it.

grounded_facts: Valerie Monroe shifts his performance focus to sing directly to Reese North, indicating a personal and intimate connection amid the public setting.
memories.memory_text: Valerie Monroe turned and sang directly to me, locking his focus on me amid the Graham Finch, making it feel intimate and personal even in that noisy, public place.

grounded_facts: Valerie Monroe articulates the idea that audience suffering leads to pleasure through catharsis, referencing ancient Greeks.
memories.memory_text: I remember Valerie Monroe explaining that the audience's suffering leads to pleasure through catharsis, like the ancient Greeks, and how their real desires are unconscious.

grounded_facts: Valerie Monroe directly asks Emery Adler if he loves the band, leading to Emery Adler affirming his affection despite his skepticism.
memories.memory_text: I was there when Valerie Monroe asked Emery Adler if he loved the band, and I heard Emery Adler say, 'I love ya. You got two more shows to do.'

grounded_facts: Post-performance gathering backstage where band members interact with Emery Adler, a manager, and each other while packing equipment.
memories.memory_text: After the performance, I stayed backstage and saw the band talking with Emery Adler and the manager while they packed up the equipment.

grounded_facts: Manager promotes a commercially viable music direction, suggesting lighter tunes for radio success.
memories.memory_text: I was told by the manager that he loved our music but thought some of it was too dark, and he suggested we should make lighter tunes like Herman's Hermits to get more radio play.

grounded_facts: Jesse Sawyer informs the manager that all band decisions require full agreement among the four members.
memories.memory_text: I saw Jesse Sawyer tell the manager that the band would only make decisions if all four of us agreed, and that they’d have a meeting before doing anything.

grounded_facts: Reese North calls her friends, urging them to attend and specifically request Valerie Monroe.
memories.memory_text: I called my friends and urged them to come see Valerie Monroe, making sure they knew to ask for him by name.

memories.memory_text: I remember Valerie Monroe insisting we all take peyote together in the Cedar Grove Park to reach a deeper stage, and I told him I was ready — I wanted to go and do the good peyote with him.

grounded_facts: Valerie Monroe dismisses Caprice's name as dumb after she gives it in response to his question.

memories.memory_text: I heard Caprice ask Valerie Monroe to leave her name at the door for entry to the show.

memories.memory_text: I was with Valerie Monroe on the Sunset Strip near the Whisky a Go Go before their show, and I remember pulling him away while he exchanged a look with someone, then the Graham Finch giggling as he climbed a pole and yelled.

grounded_facts: Valerie Monroe climbs a pole and demands the Graham Finch affirm they are alive, testing their awareness and connection.
memories.memory_text: I saw Valerie Monroe climb the pole and shout at the Graham Finch, demanding to know if anyone really felt alive—he kept urging people to raise their hands, and eventually a few did, smiling as if waking up.

grounded_facts: A psychedelic gathering in the Cedar Grove Park where Summit Council and others ingest peyote and undergo intense psychological and spiritual experiences.
memories.memory_text: I was in a circle with everyone in the Cedar Grove Park, laughing at first, but then I started vomiting and felt completely overwhelmed while Sawyer Arden tried to comfort me.

grounded_facts: Valerie Monroe reassures Reese North after she vomits, telling her the experience will improve.
memories.memory_text: I was so sick, vomiting on the edge of the cliff, and Valerie Monroe came up to me, hugged me, and told me it would get better.

grounded_facts: Valerie Hart expresses overwhelming fear of infinite personal freedom and lack of external validation, revealing deep psychological distress.
memories.memory_text: I heard Valerie Hart break down, crying about how scared he was of having too many choices and that no one would care if he died.

grounded_facts: In response to Valerie Hart's fear of infinite choice, Valerie Monroe coldly tells him to die, shocking Jonah Winslow.
memories.memory_text: I saw Valerie Monroe coldly tell Valerie Hart to die, and I felt the shock in the air when Jonah Winslow reacted with disbelief.

grounded_facts: Valerie Monroe tells Reese North he loves her after she expresses identity confusion between astrological signs.
memories.memory_text: I told Valerie Monroe I didn't know who I was, caught between being wild and safe, and then he said, 'I love you.'

grounded_facts: Valerie Monroe interprets Jonah Winslow's lust as guilt-driven and urges him to 'fuck death away,' reframing desire as rebellion.
memories.memory_text: I heard Valerie Monroe tell Jonah Winslow that his lust was really about guilt, like being a good Catholic, and he told him to 'fuck death away' as a way to rebel.

grounded_facts: Valerie Monroe responds to Valerie Hart's fear of his father and Yahweh by urging him to kill his father, citing past abuse.
memories.memory_text: I remember Valerie Hart confessing his fear of his father and Yahweh, and then Valerie Monroe telling him to kill his father because he'd tried to kill him first.

memories.memory_text: I saw Jonah Winslow admit he was scared and felt blindness coming on, saying he didn’t think he could make it through the experience.

grounded_facts: Valerie Monroe physically and emotionally draws Jonah Winslow into the group circle, promising solidarity and shared spiritual journey.

grounded_facts: Valerie Monroe delivers a visionary metaphor about confronting a cosmic serpent as a path to freedom, framing fear and transcendence as necessary.
memories.memory_text: I think Valerie Monroe was trying to say something about facing a cosmic serpent to be free, but I couldn't understand it—he just walked away as I was calling out for him, and I felt like he left me behind.

grounded_facts: As Valerie Monroe walks away alone, Reese North screams for him to come dance, expressing desperation and abandonment.
memories.memory_text: I called out to Valerie Monroe, begging him to come back and dance with me, but he kept walking—I screamed because I couldn't bear being left behind.

grounded_facts: Valerie Monroe breaks from the group and admits to himself that he is scared, revealing vulnerability after leading the group through an intense psychedelic experience.
memories.memory_text: I saw Valerie Monroe break from the circle and whisper to himself that he was scared before walking into the Cedar Grove Park, his boots sinking into the sand as I watched him pull away.

grounded_facts: Emery Adler watches Valerie Monroe's performance from the balcony, shaking his head, not understanding what is happening.
memories.memory_text: I saw Emery Adler on the balcony watching Valerie Monroe's performance, shaking his head like he didn't understand what was happening.

grounded_facts: Jesse Sawyer looks at Valerie Hart with a questioning expression, signaling uncertainty about Valerie Monroe's new direction, then they decide to follow him musically.
memories.memory_text: I saw Jesse Sawyer glance at Valerie Hart with a questioning look, like he wasn't sure where Valerie Monroe was going, but then they both decided to follow along with the improvisation.

grounded_facts: Summit Council fully synchronize with Valerie Monroe’s unpredictable performance, adapting in real time to his emotional shifts and narrative turns.
memories.memory_text: I watched the band lock in together, completely in sync with Valerie Monroe's wild energy—I could feel how Jonah Winslow, Jesse Sawyer, Valerie Hart, and the others were adapting instantly to his shifts, like they were all one instrument, and it moved me deeply.

memories.memory_text: I grabbed the tambourine and shook it hard right in front of the mic, yelling 'WAKE UP!!!! HAS THIS DREAM STOPPED!!!!' — the sound ripped through the silence like a war cry.

I started speaking into the mic about heartache and the loss of God, the words spilling out — Indian ghosts, bleeding on the highway, crowding a child's mind — and I could feel the wind rising around me.
The first thing I saw was this old Indian face staring right at me—eyes locked onto mine, unblinking, like he was trying to say something I couldn’t understand.
I looked back and saw that man bleeding out on the asphalt—his guts spilling, face twisted, moaning, those wild eyes finding me again like he was still alive in the middle of dying.

I saw her—red hair like fire, moving through the Graham Finch with that Wesley Sloane—and for a second, everything stopped. Then I was walking, then running, chasing her through the noise and light, my bare feet on hot asphalt, Baudelaire still in my hand.
I scaled the tree like a cat, dropped onto her balcony, and said 'Hi...'—her eyes went wide, and I could feel her breath catch before I kissed her, soft and quick, like stealing something sacred.
I asked her name, held her eyes like I was starving for them, kissed her again—then told her mine as I backed onto the railing, and when she whispered 'Reese North,' it felt like we'd already begun.

I watched their faces from under my hood—groaning, hissing, laughing—while my voice talked about God and mandalas and fucking the sun, and all they saw was a guy on a hash pipe winking at them like a joke.
I said 'I quit'—just like that—and walked out while the room was still yelling, didn't look back, could feel Jesse Sawyer behind me maybe saying something, but I was already gone.
I was laughing, grabbing the wheel, yanking Jesse Sawyer’s hair—let’s go, man, let’s drive to Mexico, full speed, no rules, the road’s ours!
I rolled down the window and started crawling out—wind screaming, cars blurring—freedom right there, and they were all screaming, grabbing my legs, trying to pull me back into the cage.

I slid her door open and crawled up beside the bed—she was sleeping there with him, so still—and I reached out and touched her toe, just to feel if she was real. When she jerked awake and said 'You're crazy!', I smiled because I knew she’d remember that touch.

I remember the way the firelight flickered on Reese North’s face when she asked if I was a shaman—like she was half-afraid, half-hopeful. I just said no, I only write about it, but the silence after felt heavy, like I’d denied something I couldn’t name.
I laughed and pulled Valerie Hart close, saying we should take Tijuana acid, start a religion, or plan a murder—just throwing it all out there to feel the spark, to see who’d catch fire.
I was singing with my back to them, feeling the words pull me inward, like I was chasing the sound into some dark corner only I could see.
I spun around hard, slamming my body into the mic stand, rubbing against it like it meant something — and then I saw Reese North, really saw her, and the song wasn’t mine anymore, it was hers.

I told Emery Adler, 'The greater the suffering, the more terrible the events, the greater the pleasure — they want it, it's catharsis,' and he just scratched his head like I was some freak, but then he said he loved us, so I knew he got it.
I jumped through traffic, horns blaring, and told the band we all had to take peyote together—it wasn't just a trip, it was a ceremony, the next stage, more than music, more than us.

Standing there, the Graham Finch's laughter fading, I heard the rattle of a gourd, then the drum—like Arizona—and suddenly 'The End' was in my head, rising up from somewhere ancient, like the Cedar Grove Park was speaking through me.
I saw the truck flipped over, bodies just lying there in the road, so still, and I couldn’t look away.
The dying Indian man looked at me, and I looked into his eyes — I don’t know how long, but I felt it.

I stood there surrounded by those ancient petroglyphs—buffalo, deer, masked gods—and then I saw it: an eagle-faced deity staring straight through me, like it knew me. The air changed, and I felt something watching, something alive in the rock itself.

A large lizard with tattered skin and black, pearly eyes stared at me. Then the ghost appeared—a blur of light with a headdress and skins—looking at me. It spoke in an old, familiar voice, calling me a prince among white men and a warrior among them. It told me to walk with the pain of the world. I didn’t know what it meant, but I knew I had seen and heard something real.

I felt the heat of every eye in the room burning into me as I gripped the mic, sweat stinging my eyes, and whispered those words—'Father... I want to kill you'—like a confession torn from my Tristan Vale.
After the last note cracked from my throat, I screamed—something raw and wordless tore out of me, and then I felt my body go loose, like strings were cut, like I wasn’t holding anything anymore.

I remember shouting at Emery Adler, 'Hey, is that asshole gonna pay us?' right after they threw us out—my body still burning from being dragged down the stairs, but I had to know we’d get what we were owed.

I swung across the stage like Tarzan, rope in hand, flying into the roar of the Graham Finch — then dropped down and hit the mic with 'The time to hesitate is through,' my voice cracking the night open.

I let go — completely — floating over the Graham Finch, limp in their hands, spotlight flickering across my face as girls kissed me and the men roared; I was no longer me, just a body passing through fire.
I pressed my face to the airplane window, hugging Reese North close, and told her I wouldn’t mind dying in a the small case crash with a smile on my face—death should be felt, not dragged out.

I sang 'Come on baby, light my fire' not just to end the song, but to burn it all down — the rules, their control, the whole damn cage — and when I dropped to the floor, I felt the rush of being finally free, even if the camera couldn't find me.
They had me spreadeagled against the wall, laughing while one reached under, spreading my ass, asking where the roach powder was—like I was some filthy joke.
After the Redwood Press hit me and I fell, I remember whispering from the floor—'You better kill me, cause I'm gonna come back and fuck every one of your daughters'—and meaning it.
I sat there drinking, coughing ugly, and told them I was a joke the gods played — a fake hero with the soul of a clown — and for the first time, I said it without flinching, almost smiling.

I leaned in and spoke about Texas Radio and the big beat like it was a message from the edge of everything — cold, divine, urgent — because out there on the perimeter, there are no stars, only us, stoned and awake in the dark.
I heard her scream that she fucked someone to hurt me, and I just stayed silent—my body rigid, my jaw clenched—then let the music rise up like a wall between us.
I slammed my shot glass down and told Blair Sawyer to cut the melodrama—he wasn't fun anymore, none of it was. Then I said it plain: 'I got an idea Blair Sawyer, you're fired.'
When Blair Sawyer screamed we'd be dead without the tour, I just looked at him and said, 'I care'—not loud, but heavy, like it meant more than it sounded.

I'm sitting there coughing, the judge's voice drones like it's from another planet, and all I can think is 'I can't believe this is happening'—the room feels like a fever dream, all washed-out light and sweating faces, like we're already ghosts.

memories.memory_text: I walked into the house and left him behind, the music swallowing me whole, people laughing, moving—I didn’t look back.
I felt a touch on my toe, cold and sudden, and jolted awake to see Valerie Monroe there in the dark, crawling next to my bed—my heart slammed into my chest and I screamed, 'You're crazy!'

I told Valerie Monroe I lost my Eastgate Heights on the Northbridge Warehouse yesterday—I left it somewhere and couldn’t remember where, and when I went back, it was gone. I started talking about my sister too, my voice shaking, everything piling up at once.
I broke into sobs and leaned into him, needing to be held—just needing someone—and he hugged me. I didn’t pull away. I let him hold me.
He turned and sang right to me, like the noise and all those people vanished — I felt his voice lock into my chest, and for a second, I was the only one in the room.
I said it right there on the Sunset Strip—I want to, I'm ready—because I wanted to go to the Cedar Grove Park with Valerie Monroe and take the peyote.
I was vomiting on the edge of the cliff, and Sawyer Arden was trying to comfort me. Valerie Monroe came up, we hugged, and then I threw up again.
I was dancing alone on the dune. Sand fell from my hand. Valerie Monroe was nearby, then left to look at a bird, then rejoined the others.
I ran that flower under Valerie Monroe’s nose and through his hair, making silly faces at him until he started laughing, and then I tripped him—just like that, right there on the grass.
I took off running and he came after me, chasing me across the lawn, the camera still rolling—I could hear him behind me, and I was laughing so hard I could barely breathe.

I was cutting Valerie Monroe's food while he pressed his face to the airplane window, hugging me, saying he'd want to die in a the small case crash with a smile—like it was romantic. I couldn't believe it, I just said, 'As compared to what?' because the whole thing felt so wrong, so twisted.

I saw that girl squeeze through the Graham Finch and just glue herself to Valerie Monroe, her lips on his, hands clawing at his pants—like he was some animal to be torn apart—and I burned up inside, furious, helpless, watching him smile like he liked it.
I saw her walk past me, that girl leaving Valerie Monroe’s side, and our eyes locked — I could feel the jealousy burning in my chest, hot and sharp.
I tried to take the bottle from him, and he fought me for it—'No!!!!! Mommy!!!'—and I just snapped, screaming 'Give it to me!!!' before giving up and heading for the door.
When I said I was leaving, he grabbed me and we crashed into the lamp, and then he started yelling about other men and who I'd slept with, all wild and twisted, like he wasn't even seeing me anymore.

I was laughing, introducing Jamie Nolan and Sawyer Bennett Ruspoli to Valerie Monroe. I said Sawyer Bennett was from a famous Italian family, seven hundred years old. I touched Valerie Monroe’s arm and asked if he liked the way Sawyer Bennett talked.

I was laughing, stumbling down the red carpet with a champagne bottle, and then suddenly Valerie Monroe wasn't there anymore — I looked around and he was gone, just empty white Summit Council stretching forever.

I saw her—Elliot Monroe—on her knees, that blonde head buried in his leather pants, and Valerie Monroe just pinned there, smiling like he didn’t even see me. I screamed, hands flying to my face, like if I couldn’t see it, it wasn’t happening.

I was hitting him—wild, desperate punches—and he just stood there laughing, that doped smile on his face. Everyone was laughing—Elliot Monroe, the people in the hall, the whole world—it felt like I was the only one who was real.
I squeezed Valerie Monroe’s hand—soft, quick—no words, just that. For a second, none of the fighting mattered.
I handed Valerie Monroe the list—safflower oil, Gravy Train for Skyler Colter—and told him I’d meet him up front, watching him shuffle off like a sleepwalker through the aisles.

At the register, I asked him if he had cash, and he just stood there fumbling, pulling out a crumpled dollar and a credit card, then started drawing on his own face in the magazine like it meant something.

I was so angry when I saw Valerie Monroe spacing out again—he promised he wouldn’t take acid before the dinner, and I’d made the duck, people were coming, and all he could do was whisper and giggle like a kid. I yelled, 'What the hell are you on?' because I couldn’t stand how he kept breaking his word.

After he kissed me and sang that poem, I felt it again—the pull, the romance, like we were the only two people in the world. I took the acid from his hand and said, 'I like it when you sing to me,' because in that moment, I wanted to fall into him, into the trip, into whatever madness he was offering.

I told Valerie Monroe right then, in front of everyone, that I was going to be his editor — really serious — I’d organize all his papers, take out the fuck words, make sense of it all. I could see the duck was burned, everything was chaos, and he was just laughing.

People kept coming, knocking, peering in — Jesse Sawyer, Sawyer Arden, Valerie Hart, Jonah Winslow, all these strangers — and I couldn’t focus, everything was noise and movement, like they were judging me. I just kept thinking: this is supposed to be our home, our moment, and now it’s all slipping.

I was lying there, half out of it, Sawyer Bennett next to me, and then suddenly Valerie Monroe was in the doorway—just standing there, looking at me like I was already gone. I barely got out a 'Hi' before everything turned cold.
I felt the lighter fluid soaking through the door, then the heat—oh god, the heat—when he lit it, and I screamed his name, raw and desperate, as the flames started crawling under the crack.
I kicked and kicked until my shoulder cracked, until the frame splintered—I burst out just as the flames roared behind me, gasping, my skin screaming, but alive.
I ran out into Laurel Canyon, my heart pounding, like a deer fleeing a fire—I couldn't stay there one more second.
I was begging Valerie Monroe at the door, my mascara running down my face, just needing to get in—'Valerie Monroe, I gotta talk! Let me in please!' I could feel it, he wasn’t alone.

I pressed my ear to the door and knew—just knew—someone else was in there with him. 'Valerie Monroe, I know there's someone in there,' I said, the disgust rising in my throat. How could he do this again?

I watched Valerie Monroe sitting there, coughing, bearded, smoking, looking broken while the judge read the charges—he looked like a ghost of himself, and I couldn’t speak, couldn’t move, just sat there burning inside.
I was screaming at Valerie Monroe, begging him to come back from the edge—my voice raw, the wind tearing the words out of me, but he just laughed and pretended to fall.
I climbed out onto the narrow ledge, skirts whipping in the wind, high and shaking, shouting that I loved him—I had to reach him, touch him, stop him from falling or jumping.

memories.memory_text: I leaned over to Valerie Monroe in that packed screening room and told him his film was great, that it was non-linear, it was poetry—Godard stuff—right after everyone started booing and hissing like they’d seen something obscene.
I was pounding out 'Gloria' on the piano, going full Emery Adler Lee Lewis, loud and wild, even though I could feel the others wincing at my warbling or the feedback screeching through the room.

I was fighting to keep control of the wheel while Valerie Monroe lunged over, yanking my hair and trying to steer us into Mexico—his laughter raw in my ears, the Eastgate Heights swerving through traffic.
I saw his waist disappear out the window—Jonah Winslow screaming—he was really going to jump, and I screamed 'GET HIM BACK IN!' like it might pull him back from the edge.

I was meditating on the rooftop, frowning and shaking my head because the peace wasn't coming. Then I opened my eyes and saw Valerie Monroe standing over me, slouched with the sun behind him. I said, 'Valerie Monroe... Aw shit.'

I had to stop Valerie Monroe mid-song—his timing was dragging, throwing the whole groove off. I told him straight: 'Stay with the beat, Valerie Monroe,' because the fire in the music starts with discipline.

Once Valerie Hart played the chords, I heard the solos unfolding—jazz changes, shifting time signatures. I told the others to leave so I could work it out alone, needing space to shape the song’s spine: 'Give me some space. Come on! Go!'
I was pacing inside, fingers tapping the piano keys, and when the riff finally hit me, I had to shout—'I got it!'—they needed to hear it now, no more fooling around on the beach.
I cued them like a conductor—'Bach and Rock. Sawyer Bennett it off'—and then my hands found the keys, that opening riff rising like fire, pulling everyone in.
I shouted at Valerie Monroe to turn around, to let the audience in — he was facing away again, lost in himself while people barely noticed us.

The manager handed me his card, promising real equipment, a demo, even roadies if we signed a five-year contract, but I told him we’d have a band meeting—what happens to one of us has to go through all of us.
I'm in pain man. I want something from the peyote. I feel the universe working perfectly, but I'm trapped inside myself—no oneness, just isolation, fear, and pain.

I remember Jonah Winslow pulling me aside, panic in his voice, saying Valerie Monroe wasn't coming—but I held firm, telling him Blair Sawyer was with him, that they were just an hour out.
I said 'the wine man, the ancient wine'—something Valerie Monroe once told us about Dionysos, when the madness took over. It just came out, like a whisper, almost to myself.

I was arguing with the Jordan Vaughn about the missing seats and the Graham Finch. He said he removed the seats to fit more people. Blair Sawyer wanted to cancel the show, but the Jordan Vaughn threatened to keep our gear if we didn’t play.

Jonah Winslow was shaking, ready to bolt—he wouldn’t go on unless Valerie Monroe stayed under control. I pulled him aside, held him back, begged him to just get through tonight. I promised we’d deal with it tomorrow, but right then, all I could do was keep him from walking out.

I saw Reese North start climbing out onto the ledge, skirts flapping in the wind, screaming that she loved him—Valerie Monroe egging her on—and my chest locked up, thinking she might fall, that any second she’d slip and we’d lose her too.

I couldn't just stand there watching them film it like it was entertainment—Baker and the crew swishpanning with that damn camera—so I moved toward them, voice breaking as I shouted, trying to stop the madness before someone died.

I remember the sound rising, all of us locked in—fingers moving, the room vibrating, Reese North’s hair swinging like a metronome to our pulse. It felt like we were finally becoming something real, even without Valerie Monroe there.
I offered to play the new mixes of 'LA WOMAN' while Valerie Monroe was surrounded by the kids, trying to pull the moment toward my work, toward something real we’d built.
